senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to engage in doing what is good

senses.subdomain: Kinship Relations of the Same Generation
senses.def: a female having the same father and mother as the reference person
senses.comment: For a discussion of ἀδελφή[a] in the possible meaning of cousin, see the discussion under ἀδελφός[a] (10.49).|A number of languages make a distinction in relative age of sisters, paralleling the usage of distinct terms for ‘brother’ (see 10.49). The order of names in the NT normally suggests relative age, and therefore in speaking of Martha and Mary in such languages, one may designate Mary as the younger sister, since the order is normally first Martha and then Mary, though in John 11:1 the order is reversed.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a close female associate of a group with well-defined membership (in the NT referring specifically to fellow believers in Christ)
senses.comment: Though in a number of languages it is possible to use a term meaning ‘sister’ in the sense of a fellow believer, in some languages this cannot be done. As in the case of ἀδελφός[b] (see 11.23), it may be possible to use a term such as ‘relative,’ but more often than not, it may be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘one who also believes’ or ‘one who believes in Christ even as we do.’

senses.def: to lift up and carry (away)
to destroy, with the implication of removal and doing away with
to deprive a person of life, with the implication of this being the result of condemnation by legal or quasi-legal procedures
to withdraw money from a bank
(an idiom, literally: to take from) to cause someone to no longer experience something
(an idiom, literally: to lift up the soul of someone) to keep someone in suspense so that one cannot come to a conclusion in one’s thinking
glosses: to keep someone from being able to form a conclusion about something

senses.def: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to take up one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
glosses: to be prepared to suffer even unto death
senses.comment: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.

senses.def: an idiom, literally: to lift up voice
glosses: to speak in a loud voice

senses.def: a jar made of alabaster stone
senses.comment: An alabaster jar normally had a rather long neck which was broken off for the contents to be used. It served primarily as a container for precious substances such as perfumes.|In translating ‘alabaster jar’ many translators have simply used a term meaning ‘jar’ or ‘flask’ and have either employed a descriptive qualifier, for example, ‘made of alabaster stone’ or ‘made of valuable stone’ or ‘made of valuable stone called alabaster.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being without fault or blame
to observe closely and give serious consideration to, suggesting the possibility of something unusual
senses.comment: In Acts 17:23 ἀναθεωρέω implies considerable mental activity, for Paul was not merely looking at the objects of worship but was undoubtedly thinking about the implications of them. In fact, in some languages it may be necessary to specify the elements of seeing and thinking by translating ‘for as I walked around and saw your objects of worship and thought about them.’

senses.def: to continue to think back upon
senses.comment: In a number of instances the equivalent of ‘think back on’ is ‘think about what happened’ or ‘reflect about what happened some time ago.’

senses.def: to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs
senses.comment: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be trained at the feet of) to be given extensive and formal instruction by someone
glosses: to be educated under the direction of
senses.comment: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of this part of Acts 22:3 is simply ‘Gamaliel was his teacher.’

senses.def: pertaining to what is not consecrated or devoted to God
pertaining to being tender (yielding readily to pressure)
(an idiom, literally: putting off of the dwelling, 7.8) euphemistic expression for dying
(a technical, legal term) to pay compensation for damages or costs
senses.comment: It is also possible to translate this expression in Philemon 1:19 as ‘I will pay you for any loss which you have had.’

senses.def: to plow, as a means of preparing land for sowing
senses.comment: In biblical times plows did not turn over the soil but were used simply to break the surface, seldom to a depth of more than about ten inches (or twenty five centimeters).

senses.def: pertaining to being not only dark, but also dirty and miserable
senses.comment: In 2 Peter 1:19 αὐχμηρός may also suggest moral degradation, and in English the phrase ‘filthy darkness’ could suggest this type of meaning.

senses.def: a prisoner released by Pilate at the request of the Jews during the trial of Jesus

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: beryl, usually bluish green or green in color (see 2.29)

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: to cause a forceful and abundant supply of a liquid
senses.comment: This flow from a spring may be referred to in some languages as ‘to cause to come out’ or ‘to cause to flow out.’

senses.def: to engage in agriculture or gardening
(derivative of Δαμασκός ‘Damascus,’ 93.459) a person who lives in or is a native of Damascus
a silversmith in Ephesus
a church leader
to be thoroughly perplexed
glosses: to not know what to do

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: the act of doing what God requires
causing someone to be in a proper or right relation with someone else
glosses: causing to be in a right relationship with
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, interpret δικαιόω, δικαίωσις, and δικαιοσύνη in the following contexts as meaning forensic righteousness, that is to say, the act of being declared righteous on the basis of Christ’s atoning ministry; but it would seem more probable that Paul uses these expressions in the context of the covenant relation rather than in the context of legal procedures.|It may be difficult in some languages to find a succinct expression equivalent to ‘to be put right with.’ Sometimes the closest equivalent may be ‘to be related to as one should be.’ In some instances the implication of a right relationship may be expressed by phrases involving ‘acceptance.’ For example, Romans 3:24 may be expressed as ‘by the free gift of God’s grace they are accepted by him through Christ Jesus who sets them free.’ Similarly, Romans 4:25 is sometimes expressed as ‘he was raised to life in order to cause us to be accepted by God.’ There are, however, certain dangers involved in terms indicating ‘acceptance,’ since this might imply God’s reluctance to accept people apart from the atoning work of Jesus Christ, while in reality it was God who was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. Therefore, one should clearly avoid a rendering which would seem to suggest different types of motivation in the Godhead.|Some scholars, however, understand the phrase δικαιοσύνη θεοῦ in Romans 1:17 as referring to God’s faithfulness to his promises made to Abraham. In other words, the focus would be upon God’s moral integrity, but it is difficult to relate this interpretation to the statement about faith in Romans 1:17b.

senses.def: observances or practices required by one’s religion
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand δικαιοσύνη in Matthew 6:1 as meaning ‘alms’ (see 57.111).

senses.def: giving to those in need as an act of mercy
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret δικαιοσύνη in Matthew 6:1 as ‘religious observances’ (see 53.4).

senses.def: an elaborate meal
to dress oneself, with the implication of clothing which is tied on
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 5:5 ἐγκομβόομαι is used figuratively, and one may render it as ‘to show’ or ‘to demonstrate.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: duration of time, with reference to a series of occasions
to fall from a particular point or location
(a technical, nautical term) to drift off or be blown off one’s course and hence run aground
glosses: to be blown off course and run aground

senses.def: to abandon a former relationship or association, or to dissociate (a type of reversal of beginning to associate)
senses.comment: Note, however, that the underlying structure of the expression τῆς χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε really involves ‘turning away from God who has shown grace.’ For another interpretation of ἐκπίπτω in Galatians 5:4, see 90.72.

senses.def: to change for the worse, with emphasis upon extent and suddenness
(figurative extension of meaning of ἐκπίπτω[a] ‘to fall out or from,’ 15.120) to become inadequate for some function
to no longer experience a state or condition
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐκπίπτω in Galatians 5:4, see 34.26.

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:14)
ninth in a series involving either time, space, or set

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to live a life of luxury, usually associated with intemperate feasting and drinking
glosses: to live a life of luxury

senses.def: to force someone or something to leave
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to indicate more explicitly the factors involved in driving out the nations, for example, ‘the nations whom God forced to leave their land as our ancestors came in.’

senses.def: the movement of a ship being driven ashore
glosses: to run a ship onto a beach

senses.def: pertaining to being located on the earth
pertaining to human, earthly activity (primarily in contrast with divine activity)
to come to dwell in a place defined psychologically or spiritually (with the possible implication in some contexts of a temporary arrangement)
senses.comment: In their NT contexts, σκηνόω and ἐπισκηνόω are essentially figurative in meaning, for they deal with spiritual existence and residence rather than human residence or dwelling. In translating one should, in so far as possible, try to preserve this important figurative relationship, since it expresses one of the most significant ways in which spiritual and human existence can be combined. In some languages, however, it may be necessary to employ an expression which means simply ‘to be in’ or ‘to continue with,’ since expressions for ‘living’ or ‘dwelling’ may be based upon terms which are too specific in meaning, for example, ‘to eat from the same pot’ or ‘to enter by the same door.’

senses.subdomain: Areas Which Are Uninhabited or Only Sparsely Populated
senses.def: a largely uninhabited region, normally with sparse vegetation (in contrast with πόλις[a] ‘a population center,’ 1.88)
senses.comment: The phrase ἄνυδρος τόπος (Matthew 12:43, Luke 11:24), literally ‘waterless place,’ is a set phrase equivalent to ἐρημία and may be translated as ‘wilderness’ or ‘uninhabited country.’|Throughout the NT ἐρημία and ἔρημος[b] focus primarily upon the lack of population rather than upon sparse vegetation, though the two features are closely related ecologically in the Middle East.|In most languages the most satisfactory equivalent of ἐρημία and ἔρημος[b] is a word or phrase suggesting a place where few if any people live. Such expressions are generally far better than a word meaning ‘a bare place’ or ‘a place of sand,’ since in some languages such expressions could mean only a clearing in the forest or a sandy beach along a river bank. In the case of translations being made for people living in jungle areas, it may, however, be necessary to describe in a footnote the nature of an ἐρημία in NT times.

senses.def: pertaining to being encouraged

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: a single occurrence
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐφάπαξ in 1 Corinthians 15:6, see 67.34.

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: a single occurrence to the exclusion of any other similar occurrence
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘once and for all’ is simply ‘once and not again’ or ‘once and not twice.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time which is emphatically simultaneous with another point of time
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐφάπαξ in 1 Corinthians 15:6, see 60.67.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: the period of time when a person is alive
senses.comment: In Matthew 6:27 ἡλικία may also denote height (see 81.4). If one understands ἡλικία in Matthew 6:27 as time, then obviously some adjustment needs to be made to the meaning of πῆχυς ‘cubit’ (81.25). For many languages the most appropriate term is one which means ‘day,’ but it would also be possible to use some other unit of length if this would clearly imply an impossibility.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: the period of life when one is mature and at one’s prime
senses.comment: Normally the phrase παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας (Hebrews 11:11) would refer to a woman beyond menopause.

senses.def: height as the dimension of stature of an animate object
pertaining to fighting against God
glosses: to be an enemy of God
senses.comment: Although the figurative expression ‘fighting against God’ is an unusual and radical figure of speech, it can often be translated more or less literally, but in some languages such an expression is regarded as both impossible and even ludicrous, and therefore one must employ some such expression as ‘to be a constant enemy of God’ or ‘to be always against God.’

senses.def: an opening in a wall for the entrance of light and air and for the purpose of seeing in or out
a seaport on the coast of Palestine
a marker of similarity in events and states, with the possible implication of something being in accordance with something else

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to a positive moral quality, with the implication of being favorably valued
pertaining to having acceptable characteristics or functioning in an agreeable manner, often with the focus on outward form or appearance
pertaining to providing some special or superior benefit
pertaining to being fitting and at the same time probably good
pertaining to being beautiful or attractive in terms of outward form or shape, often implying a corresponding fine value

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to having high status, with the possible implication of its attractiveness
to come/go behind or after, with the possible implication of continual and determined action
to drag or lead, with emphasis upon forceful and thorough action

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being proud without basis or justification
senses.comment: It is often possible to render ‘to be falsely proud’ as ‘to be proud when there is no reason to be proud’ or ‘to be proud even when there is nothing to be proud of.’

senses.def: (derivative of κληρονομέω[a] ‘to gain as a possession,’ 57.131) a valuable possession which has been received
(derivative of κληρονομέω[b] ‘to inherit,’ 57.138) that which is received from a deceased person
senses.comment: In Luke 12:13 it may also be possible to render κληρονομία as ‘the property our father left us’ or ‘the property which our father said should be given to us.’

senses.def: the leader of a rebellion against Moses
to move in such a way as to encircle an object
a relatively small part which continues to exist
a city southeast of Joppa
wealth and riches, with a strongly negative connotation
to bring accusations against someone on the basis that the person in question is clearly to blame
a combination of the negative particle μή[a] ‘not,’ 69.3, and the somewhat emphatic postpositional particle γέ, 91.6; these are often written separately
a place where one may remain or dwell

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a period of time when one is young

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse
a fermented beverage made from the juice of grapes
senses.comment: Though some persons have argued that whenever mention is made of Jesus either making or drinking wine, one must assume that this was only unfermented grape juice, there is no real basis for such a conclusion. Only where οἶνος νέος ‘new wine’ (6.198) is mentioned can one assume that this is unfermented grape juice or grape juice in the initial stages of fermentation.|In a number of languages there is no indigenous term for wine, and some expression may simply be borrowed from a dominant language. On the other hand, it is sometimes possible to employ a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘fermented fruit juice.’ In some languages the equivalent for ‘wine’ is more specifically ‘palm wine,’ that is to say, a wine made from the sap of certain palm trees. Such a term may also have a more generic meaning and be applicable to any kind of wine.|There are a number of passages in the NT where one must be particularly careful in the selection of terms to translate wine. For example, in Ephesians 5:18 a literal translation of ‘do not get drunk with wine’ could be interpreted to mean that it is permissible for one to get drunk on other types of intoxicating liquors. It may, therefore, be necessary in some languages to render Ephesians 5:18 as simply ‘do not get drunk.’|In Luke 10:34 (κατέδησεν τὰ τραύματα αὐτοῦ ἐπιχέων ἔλαιον καὶ οἶνον ‘he poured on olive oil and wine and bandaged his wounds’) it is important to recognize the medicinal value of oil and wine. In some instances translators have indicated the purpose of such an activity by translating ‘to cleanse and heal his wounds he poured wine and oil on them and bandaged them.’ It may also be possible to add in a marginal note information as to the antiseptic quality of the wine and the value of the oil in the healing process.

senses.def: a set phrase referring to newly pressed grape juice, unfermented or in the initial stages of fermentation
a set phrase referring to wine drugged with myrrh and used as a stupefying potion
senses.comment: In general, ἐσμυρνισμένος οἶνος must be rendered by means of a phrase or a clause, for example, ‘wine which has been mixed with a drug called myrrh’ or ‘wine mixed with a drug to reduce pain.’ It is, of course, also possible to use an abbreviated phrase such as ‘myrrhed wine’ and then to place the explanation of its function in a marginal note.

senses.def: an opening or hole in the ground, either large as in Hebrews 11:38 or relatively small as in James 3:11
senses.comment: Holes would differ from caves (Hebrews 11:38) in that holes would be vertical openings into the ground, while caves would be more or less horizontal openings into cliffs or sides of hills. In James 3:11 it may be quite unnecessary, and in fact confusing, to try to translate ὀπῆς, since ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς ὀπῆς ‘from the same opening’ would seem to be redundant with ἡ πηγή ‘spring,’ since a spring would presumably only flow from a hole or opening in the ground.

senses.def: an exclamation of mocking and ridicule
senses.comment: Almost all languages have interjections or exclamatory expressions indicating ridicule. If such does not exist in a language, one can always translate this expression in Mark 15:29 as ‘now what about you, you who are going to destroy the sanctuary and in three days build it up again!’

senses.def: to experience a complete change in one’s way of life to what it should be, with the implication of return to a former state or relation
senses.comment: The metaphor of ‘new birth’ is so important in the NT that it should be retained if at all possible. In some languages ‘new birth’ can be expressed as ‘to cause to be born all over again’ or ‘to have a new life as though one were born a second time.’ See also 13.55.

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an era involving the renewal of the world (with special reference to the time of the Messiah)
to act contrary to established custom or law, with the implication of intent
senses.comment: Languages differ appreciably in the way in which they speak of disobeying or transgressing a law. It is rarely possible to speak of ‘breaking a law,’ since nothing is actually done to the law in the process of transgression, but languages do employ such expressions as ‘to tramp on a law,’ ‘to ridicule a law,’ and ‘to laugh at a law.’ See also discussion at 36.29.

senses.def: a relatively flat dish, probably somewhat smaller than a πίναξ (6.134); made of baked clay or metal
senses.comment: In this one NT context in which παροψίς occurs, it seems to refer to any kind of plate or dish, though in contexts outside the NT, παροψίς is often employed to refer to a dish used for serving certain choice foods and delicacies.

senses.def: to shine very brightly on an area surrounding an object
senses.comment: See the discussion in 14.44.

senses.def: a large plank at the stern of a ship used to direct its course
senses.comment: For some ships the rudder may have been simply a large steering paddle. For languages which have no technical term, a rudder may be described as ‘an instrument for steering the ship’ or ‘an instrument for making the ship go the way one wants it to go.’

senses.def: the movement of a boat or ship through the water, either rowed or blown by the wind

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no special color term for reddish-purple, since the color in question is sometimes classified as a kind of blue and in other instances it is related to black. However, in all languages it is possible to be somewhat more precise about color terms by likening the color to that of a local flower or bird.

senses.def: to hope in a prior manner, either beforehand or prior to someone else
glosses: to be the first to hope

senses.def: to speak to or to make requests of God
senses.comment: In some languages there are a number of different terms used for prayer depending upon the nature of the content, for example, requests for material blessing, pleas for spiritual help, intercession for others, thanksgiving, and praise. There may also be important distinctions on the basis of urgency and need. The most generic expression for prayer may simply be ‘to speak to God.’ It is normally best to avoid an expression which means primarily ‘to recite.’

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to choose for a particular purpose in advance
a rod about 1-2 m. long; used for walking, herding, fighting off wild animals, beating people
senses.comment: A ῥάβδος[a] could be used for a number of different purposes, such as an aid to walking, herding animals, or beating people.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ῥάβδος ‘scepter,’ not occurring in the NT) the manner in which a person rules or governs
senses.comment: It is rare that a staff constitutes a symbol of power and therefore would have the extended meaning of ‘rule.’ Accordingly, this expression in Hebrews 1:8 must often be rendered as ‘the way in which you rule your kingdom will be righteous’ or ‘you will be righteous as you rule your kingdom.’

senses.def: a city on the southeast coast of Cyprus

senses.subdomain: Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
senses.def: the same day as the day of a discourse
a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see 14.36)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of Luke 23:44 ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of σκότος[a] ‘darkness,’ 14.53) the realm of sin and evil
senses.comment: It is possible that in Colossians 1:13 σκότος[b] is a figurative reference to the Devil or Satan, since ἐκ τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ σκότους is in a parallel relationship with τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ υἱοῦ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ.

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the gloom of darkness) the dark, gloomy nature of hell as a place of punishment

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the outer darkness) a place or region which is both dark and removed (presumably from the abode of the righteous) and serving as the abode of evil spirits and devils
senses.comment: In a number of languages this expression in Matthew 8:12 must be rendered as ‘they will be thrown outside where it is dark.’

senses.def: to put up with annoyance or difficulty
working out of a joint arrangement

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a fellow member of a socio-political unit
senses.comment: The expression in Ephesians 2:19 may also be rendered as ‘you join with God’s people as fellow citizens together with them’ or ‘you and God’s people are all persons who belong to the same place’ or as in some languages, ‘… people of God’s country.’

senses.def: to exercise continuous control over someone or something
senses.comment: There is usually no difficulty in speaking of ‘control’ if it is performed by a person as in 1 Peter 2:13. However, it may not be possible to speak of ‘death’ having control, unless the language in question can personify death. In some instances Acts 2:24 (see 37.16) must be rendered as ‘it was impossible for him to continue to be dead,’ and in 2 Corinthians 5:14 ‘Christ’s love controls us’ may be rendered as ‘the fact that Christ loves us causes us to act as we do.’

senses.def: to continue to hold in custody
senses.comment: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

senses.def: to press in hard from all sides
(an idiom, literally: to hold the ears closed) to refuse to listen to what is being said
senses.comment: In some languages the refusal to hear may be expressed idiomatically as ‘they put their hands over their ears’ or ‘they closed their ears’ or ‘the words never entered their heads.’

senses.def: to experience a state or condition, generally involving duration
to experience great psychological pressure and anxiety
to continue with close attention and devotion
glosses: to continue to give oneself to
to continue to apply oneself to

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be held together from) to be in a mental state between two alternatives
glosses: to be pulled in two directions
senses.comment: In a number of languages the rendering of this statement in Philippians 1:23 must be expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘my mind is pulling me in two directions’ or ‘my thoughts are going in two different directions’ or ‘my heart is speaking two different words to me.’

senses.def: a degree which falls just short of some point on a scale of extent
senses.comment: The equivalent of this expression in Acts 13:44 in some languages is ‘all the people in the town came, but some did not’ or ‘only a few of the people in town didn’t come.’

senses.def: to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs
senses.comment: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

senses.def: pertaining to being like some identified entity or event
a reference to that which is of such a kind as is identified in the context
glosses: of a kind such as this

senses.def: to strike or hit an object, one or more times
senses.comment: Note that the imperfect tense may be used of a repeated action, and therefore the translation ‘beat.’ ἔτυπτεν τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ ‘he beat his breast’ Luke 18:13. The action of ‘beating the breast’ in Luke 18:13 is symbolic in that it has the meaning of repentance and contrition. In other languages, however, the expression ‘to beat the breast’ may constitute a symbol of pride or self-flattery. In some languages the equivalent of the biblical expression ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to strike the head’ or ‘to grasp the abdomen.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of τύπτω[a] ‘to strike, to beat,’ 19.1) to cause serious harm to, in a psychological sense

senses.subdomain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
senses.def: to intentionally not regard or be concerned about certain objects or events
glosses: to purposely pay no attention to

senses.def: pertaining to being high
a location above the earth and associated with supernatural events or beings
senses.comment: In contexts in which these expressions refer clearly to ‘heaven’ or ‘the sky,’ it is better to use terms meaning ‘heaven’ or ‘sky’ rather than terms meaning ‘height’ or ‘that which is high.’

senses.def: pertaining to being regarded as of particular value, implying evident comparison with other items
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ὑψηλός in Luke 16:15, see 88.208.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being arrogant or proud
senses.comment: The phrase τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὑψηλόν may be rendered in some languages as ‘that which people think is great’ or ‘that which people think is very good indeed.’ For another interpretation of ὑψηλός in Luke 16:15, see 65.9.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to have an arrogant, haughty attitude
(comparative of ὑψηλός[a] ‘high,’ 81.6) a position above another, on the basis of being higher
to have love or affection for someone or something based on association
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult if not impossible to speak of ‘affection … is hostility.’ Frequently it is necessary to relate such emotional attitudes to individuals, so that this expression in James 4:4 may be rendered in some languages as ‘people who love the things in the world are against God.’|See the discussion of the meaning of φιλέω[a] and φιλία in 25.43.

senses.def: a small leather case containing OT scripture verses and worn on the arm and forehead by Jews, especially when praying
senses.comment: The Greek word φυλακτήριον, both before and during NT times, referred to an object used as a means of protection from evil forces. As such, it constituted a kind of amulet, but in Matthew 23:5 φυλακτήριον is a reference to what was called in Aramaic tephillin, meaning ‘prayers.’ The two phylacteries, one worn on the head and the other on the left arm, were bound on during daily morning prayers. Just what their function seems to have been is not certain. In Matthew 23:5, Jesus does not condemn the use of such phylacteries, but he does denounce their ostentatious use.

senses.def: a military officer, normally in command of a thousand soldiers
(derivative of ψεύδομαι ‘to lie,’ 33.253) one who utters falsehoods and lies
senses.comment: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’
